newsitem.title: UK: British shares ended rocky day sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: British shares ended rocky day sharply lower.

text.p: British shares ended a turbulent day sharply lower on Wednesday, unhinged by a plunging U.S. share market that many stockbrokers warn could be overpriced.
The Financial Times Index of the leading 100 British shares closed 53.2 points lower at 3,982.5 as investors watched U.S. shares nosedive.

The Dow industrials average of top U.S. shares was down as much as 120 points during London trading hours, crushed under the the weight of a rumour that U.S. computer giant IBM could be on the verge of issuing a profits warning.

The rumour gathered pace as IBM declined to comment on the speculation and came at a time when many stockbrokers were questioning whether or not the Dow was due for a sell-off after rising nearly 30 percent this year.

"We didn't get a meltdown today but we're not out of the woods yet," said Kirit Shah, share strategist at Japanese bank Sanwa International. "The Dow is looking overstretched and really does need to come back. If it should crash the FTSE will go down with it."
Fears that U.S. shares may be overpriced were exacerbated by press reports that Japanese investors may be on the verge of reducing their holdings in U.S. dollar assets.
Because of all of the uncertainty, Shah expects the FTSE to remain volatile in the run-up to Christmas and sees only a limited potential for share prices to rise in the short-term.
"With the prospect of rising British interest rates there is really not that much upside for the FTSE," Shah said.
The FTSE's gyrations began last Friday, when the key index plunged 88 points after U.S. central bank chairman Alan Greenspan said U.S. share prices were too high.
But the market clawed back most of those losses on Monday and Tuesday only to see the FTSE surrender a large portion of the gains on Wednesday.
"With volatility like this a lot of institutions will decide not to get involved so we could see volumes drop in the run up to Christmas," the head of trading at a large brokerage said.
"Basically, we're just going to watch Wall Street and wait. If it crashes, we'll go with it," he added.
"The only consolation is that since we haven't risen as much this year as Wall Street, we probably won't fall as far."
The FTSE 100 has risen by around nine percent in 1996, one third of the Dow's rate.
Amongst individual shares, Burmah Castrol shrugged off the general market gloom, rising 21-1/2p at 10.85 pounds and Imperial Tobacco inched 1p higher to close at 379-1/2.
